At Box, we've been testing Gemini 4 Argon on our Box AI Complex Work eval for the past week. It's a huge upgrade over Gemini 3.1 Pro, jumping by 14 percentage points across all our tests, and firmly at the frontier. 

In our evaluation, we give the Box Agent (using Gemini 4 Argon) a variety of complex enterprise tasks involving enterprise documents in a range of industries. These tasks approximate the kind of hard, time-consuming work that knowledge workers do every day with their enterprise content. Gemini 4 is a huge leap on effectively every dimension of this work.

Gemini 4 is far more capable on math, logic, analytics, and deep knowledge of a variety of business domains. It also works far harder to complete tasks fully without stopping short of the desired result. This is incredibly important for complex enterprise workflows that depend on robust task execution.

Here are some example wins that we saw to put the improvements in perspective:

* Financial services (+18 points): a funding-gap analysis for a family-owned company, where the brief spelled out every step of the projected statements, down to the interest on the bank loan and the overdraft for each year. Gemini 4 Argon built them exactly as specified, every line broken out and carried through to the funding gap. Gemini 3.1 Pro folded the interest into a single figure.

* Healthcare (+25 points): an intensive care management plan where both models spotted a dangerous potassium level and a drug interaction. Only Gemini 4 Argon went back and pulled the offending drugs from the final regimen, so its plan actually matched its own diagnosis.

* Technology (+37 points): a product performance review deciding which of two regional markets should have its cloud infrastructure optimized first. Gemini 4 Argon pulled the right month's user, retention and per-user figures for both regions and correctly flagged North America. Gemini 3.1 Pro often pulled the wrong rows, at one point reporting retention above 100%, and pointed the effort at the wrong region.

* Energy (+16 points): an energy consumption report across two facilities that had to flag any gaps in the meter data. Gemini 4 Argon consistently caught that the data center's smart meter log stops in November. Gemini 3.1 Pro often missed it, at times declaring the logs complete.

* Consumer products (+33 points): a product launch evaluation deciding which production expansion to fund. Gemini 4 Argon saw that existing inventory could bridge an early capacity gap, which made the smaller expansion viable with an earlier launch and a faster break-even. Gemini 3.1 Pro defaulted to the larger expansion and the later timeline.

Gemini 4 Argon will be available in the Box AI Studio shortly for anyone to build custom Box Agents with.

Cyber is going to be one of the biggest spaces for AI agents in the future. 

Obviously the risks of software exploits and the attack surface area increases 100 fold due to the ability for agents to work through any crack to find what they’re looking for.

But this goes the other way as well. The ability to have agent swarms review every line of code, test any number of permutations of exploits, and research any incident faster than humans as they happen, will be a huge boost in how we secure systems in the future. 

Cyber has always been a category where it’s hard to keep up with (and triage) all the incoming risks, alerts, and changes in the enterprise and across all system. You can never hire enough people or work through the backlog of all known risks. Agents actually give you a chance finally to have far better coverage of this.

This is going to be a huge opportunity as well because we’ll see plays at the labs, data providers, the layer of the network and firewall, identity, devices and endpoints, SDLC, and even how we protect our data in the enterprise. Lots of interesting dimensions to cyber at the moment.

SpaceXAI’s Grok Voice 3.0 is the new leading Speech to Speech model, debuting at #1 on the Artificial Analysis Speech to Speech Index at 86.9, while also being competitive on latency

Grok Voice 3.0 is @SpaceXSI 's successor to Grok Voice 2.0, a Speech to Speech model available through the SpaceXAI Realtime API at $0.08 per minute. We evaluated Grok Voice 3.0 with the Rex voice through the SpaceXAI Realtime API.

Key takeaways:

➤ Speech to Speech Index: Grok Voice 3.0 debuts at #1 at 86.9, ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 83.2, Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at 82.6 and GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 80.1. It is up on Grok Voice 2.0 at 81.3 (+5.6 points) and Grok Voice 1.0 at 73.7 (+13.2 points), released just under six months ago. The Index averages Speech Reasoning (Big Bench Audio), Agentic Performance (Tau Voice), Arena Preference, and Task Success Rate

➤ Speech Agent Arena: Grok Voice 3.0 ranks #3 in preference at Elo 1070, behind Gemini 3.1 Flash Live Minimal (1100) and Gemini 3.8 Live (1088) and ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 1057, and #1 on Task Success Rate at 94.8%, highest on the board, just ahead of Grok Voice 2.0 at 94.6%. Grok Voice 2.0 trails at Elo 1011

➤ Tau Voice: Grok Voice 3.0 takes the #2 spot on our Tau Voice benchmark implementation at 71.6%, behind GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 74.5% and ahead of Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at 68.6% and GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 59.3% - up from 56.5% for Grok Voice 2.0

➤ Big Bench Audio: Grok Voice 3.0 scores 98.5% on audio reasoning, ahead of Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at 97.7% and Grok Voice 2.0 at 97.2%

➤ Speed: Average Time to First Audio on Big Bench Audio is 0.81 seconds for Grok Voice 3.0, well ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 1.24s, GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 1.34s and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at 1.35s, though slower than Grok Voice 2.0 at 0.70s

➤ Cost: Grok Voice 3.0 costs $4.80 per hour of input audio, the same as Grok Voice 2.0. That is above GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at $4.47 and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at $3.50, cheaper than GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at $5.83, and ~2.2x cheaper than GPT-Realtime-2.1 High at $10.75

In addition to our new DeepSeek V4.1 Flash results, we’re adding AMD’s MI355X to AA-AgentPerf for Kimi K3, GLM-5.2/5.3 and DeepSeek V4 Pro - comparing it to our latest results for NVIDIA systems on coding agent workloads.

AA-AgentPerf is our agentic inference performance benchmark. It replays real agentic coding sessions, including prompt caching and tool-call delays, to give a realistic measure of inference performance in day-to-day agentic workloads.

MI355X is AMD's flagship accelerator in the MI350 series, launched in June 2025 on its CDNA 4 architecture. It has the same 288GB of HBM3E at 8TB/s as NVIDIA's B300, around 10 PFLOPS of dense FP4 compute (vs. B300 at ~13.5 and B200 at ~9) and board power of up to 1,400W. All our MI355X results use ROCm nightly and dev builds of vLLM and SGLang.

We are debuting results for AMD's MI355X on a single 8-GPU node across all four featured AA-AgentPerf models. Results on our leaderboard are live and will evolve over time - we look forward to tracking software/serving improvements on AMD hardware.

Initial results on MI355X:

➤ Its strongest result is on DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813, where MI355X serves ~15% to 40% more throughput per MW than B200 between 35 and 75 tok/s per user, likely helped by its 288GB of HBM per GPU (B200 has 180GB) on a 1.6T parameter model

➤ On DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, MI355X is in line with NVIDIA Blackwell for a single agent at 647 tok/s (B300 at 652, B200 at 669), but falls behind as load rises, reaching ~128M tokens/s per MW at 100 tok/s per user against ~193M for B200 and ~220M for B300

➤ On GLM-5.2/5.3, MI355X trails B200 and B300 at 100 tok/s per user, with ~26M tokens/s per MW against ~42M and ~44M respectively

➤ On Kimi K3 (2.8T parameters), MI355X serves ~8M tokens/s per MW at 50 tok/s per user against ~24M for B300 using NVIDIA's multi-node configs, and 152 tok/s for a single agent against 235

Welcome to the era of embodied AI.

We are launching AA-Robotics v0.1, our research preview that measures frontier language model performance on understanding, planning, and acting in the physical world. In v0.1, each model is given control of a 6-axis robot arm (5 joints and a gripper) and a simple objective. We’re releasing results for our first eight tasks today.

We find that frontier language models in coding agent harnesses have recently become capable of directly manipulating robot arms for simple tasks. Today, they are far too slow and expensive for any kind of production usage - nearly two orders of magnitude worse than human baselines. We expect this to change quickly.

GPT-6 Astra places first in AA-Robotics v0.1, followed by GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Argon and Claude Opus 5.5.

AA-Robotics v0.1 details:

➤ Our first eight tasks test a range of capabilities: control and dexterity (precise grasping and object handling), spatial reasoning (how objects interact with one another) and adaptability (how models respond to the unexpected)

➤ Models get only brief instructions: how to connect to the robot arm (via a simple HTTP API), the arm's name and how to submit an attempt. They can view the scene through four cameras and write and run code to plan and send movements

➤ Once a model submits an attempt, its end state is graded against the task's pass criteria. A pass scores 100; an incomplete attempt earns partial credit. All attempts are zero-shot

Key findings:

➤ The GPT family tops the leaderboard: GPT-6 Astra scores 69, ahead of GPT-6.1 Sol at 65 and Gemini 4 Argon at 55. Claude Opus 5.5 (49) and Claude Fable 5.1 (46) trail

➤ Today’s models are incredibly slow at our tasks, taking ~30 minutes on average to complete each tabletop task

➤ Cost varies widely: GPT-6.1 Sol is the cheapest at $1.93 per task on average; GPT-6 Astra, the most expensive, costs $16.36, more than eight times as much

➤ Compared with a human, today's best-performing frontier language models are ~100x slower and ~10x more expensive

More results, clips, and how AA-Robotics v0.1 works follow in the thread below

tweets.text: By the way, in my experience contractors of all sorts have adopted AI for text-based communications and it has substantially improved coordination on home renovation projects

hot AI startup character ai just filed for bankruptcy! https://t.co/TqtIm0p8LV

i gathered insights from the actual bankruptcy filing itself https://t.co/OnZvWnwe5W and this is an interesting one to break down

1. they have adoption and engagement

12M MAU, with average 2 hours of daily time spent per user! 

that’s.. quite a lot. many startup products would dream to reach this level of usage, but it didn’t work

2. they have real network effect

they have user generated characters and many users like to engage with characters made by others. so the more users they have, the richer this ecosystem becomes - textbook network effect

some people seem to think network effect is gold. nope! didn’t work

3. they have proprietary data and custom trained models

many people say software is dead and only data is moat. this gives a sobering look - private data didn’t help either

4. so what’s wrong?

they burn over $7M of compute and only get $5M of revenue per month

that’s the whole problem

people would engage for free or when subsidized, but they are not willing to pay enough $ for the value they are getting

now… the real dark side of this 

if you take a few steps back and look at all LLM usage, especially all the people on social media using tokens to make the same 3d demos every day - 

how many people are actually creating more economical value than the tokens they burnt? if there’s no subsidization and everyone has to pay at API price, how much of the current usage can actually be justified with positive ROI and sustain? 

we have limited runway to make AI work. and if we can’t, what happened to character ai may just be a preview for the entire AI industry

over the past couple of weeks, i heard multiple people telling me they could no longer use up their LLM subscriptions

the reasons were a mix of:
1. the frontier models became more efficient 
2. they felt exhausted managing agents
3. they ran out of problems that they can throw to AI

1 will continue to happen. 2 is a tooling and workflow problem (just use firstmate haha) that will be solved as well

3 is an interesting one - it points at a novelty effect that may be wearing off, and a capability gap that AI just hasn’t reached the level that most people can trust to run their daily lives yet

meanwhile, my quotas have never been tighter because i have an endless number of things i want to build

that points at the reality of user segmentation - R&D is such a niche use case that needs an astounding amount of tokens. there aren’t many other use cases that are so token intensive 

realistically, how many % of the world’s population will want to run an army of agents and build software all day? i don’t expect that to ever become a big number

so my speculation is that the current $200 subscriptions are likely already close to the ceiling of most people’s consumption needs. better models will unlock more use cases, but efficiency gains may cancel that out

like water, gas, power - most households will simply get one or two monthly AI subscription and be done

now the important part - this means if you are building a B2C business, you should almost never sell tokens as part of your offering, because there will be no demand. people already have their subscriptions and that’s enough

instead, allow people to bring their own LLM subscriptions to your product, and add value on top. i suspect this will hold for most B2B businesses as well, but for B2C this is almost certain at this point
